prose: Anil Dash (or a similar longtime Meta-watcher) lays out 'the Facebook fake-out': the cycle by which Meta ships something transgressive, weathers the outrage until attention moves on, then brings the thing back and points to the vanished backlash as proof it was fine all along. The essay frames this as part of Silicon Valley's broader 'inevitability' strategy - treating new technologies as forces of nature so society goes along with extreme plans - enabled by short attention spans, weak institutional accountability, and the coercive lock-in that makes opting out of Meta's platforms costly. Written as a reference to send to legislators and journalists 'the next time they're getting fooled by Mark Zuckerberg', and acutely relevant in the Muse era.
highlights: Names the cycle: ship the transgressive thing, wait out the outrage, reintroduce it later
Inside Meta, the moved-on public is read as proof the idea was never bad
Part of the 'inevitability' strategy: present new tech as a force of nature
Relies on short attention spans, unaccountable institutions, and lock-in coercion
Written as a reference for legislators and journalists covering Meta
Timely again as Muse's permission scandals repeat the pattern
quotes: the direct enabling of the Rohingya genocide
